title: Ang 300–317: Gauri ki Var M4
hookLine: including the Gursikh's daily routine on ang 305
tomorrow: what makes a day a good one?

lines: UP IN THE DARK WITH DAD.
cards: Morning-routine videos: the alarm at five, the cold water, the journal, the green drink, all filmed from a tripod.

Simran's dad has had a routine since before those videos existed: up in the dark, a shower, the Japji, then the yard before the trucks roll. The test is in two days, and this week Simran has been getting up with him.
Not for the drink. For the quiet. On Ang 305, in Gauri ki Var, Guru Ram Das wrote out a whole day of a Sikh of the Guru.

teach.b: In paraphrase: whoever calls themself a Sikh of the True Guru rises early and meditates on the Name. They make the effort in the early hours, bathe, and wash in the pool of nectar.
They repeat the Name as the Guru teaches, and their troubles fall away.

teach.h: THROUGH THE DAY: BREATH AND BITE.
teach.b: Then, through the day, they sing Gurbani, and with every breath and every bite, they remember. And the closing line: Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of the Gursikh who repeats the Name, and helps others repeat it too.
Notice three things. It isn't a performance; nobody's filming. It isn't only the morning; it runs through the whole day, breath and bite.
And it isn't for yourself alone; the last line is about helping someone else remember.
That's the difference between a routine and a practice.

A routine is built to improve you. This one, by the end, has turned you outward. For Simran's week, what it gives is something steady under the nerves: the day before a test starts the same way as any other.
And it closes a loop. Ang 156 was the alarm, a night lost in sleep. Ang 305 is what waking up is for.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada describes a Sikh's day much as Ang 305 does: rising early, bathing, remembering Waheguru, the morning, evening and night prayers, honest work, and sharing.

games.q: a Sikh's day on Ang 305 — tap the pairs.

s: the Gursikh's routine on Ang 305 is only about early mornings
it runs through the day: with every breath and every bite, remember.
the passage ends with Nanak asking for the dust of a Gursikh's feet
the one who repeats the Name and helps others repeat it too.
the routine is meant as proof to others that you're a real Sikh
nobody's filming: it's a practice, and it ends by helping someone else.

games.q: your friend starts a 5 a.m. routine and posts it daily. after two weeks she says it feels empty. what does Ang 305 add?
o: a practice turns outward: it runs through the day and helps someone else remember.
get up even earlier; the Gursikh's day starts before dawn.
stop posting, and the emptiness will go away by itself.
games.why: Guru Ram Das's day starts early, but it runs on through breath and bite, and its last line is about helping others repeat the Name.

practice: Plan tomorrow's first five minutes the way you'd plan a trip. Name what you want them to hold, a breath, a line, a moment of quiet, and then the one thing most likely to steal them, probably your phone.
Decide now: when I reach for it, I'll sit up and take three breaths first.
